title: Multi Location SEO: How to Manage Google Business Profiles Across Many Locations
seoTitle: Multi Location SEO: Managing Google Business Profiles
seoDescription: How to manage Google Business Profiles and local SEO across many locations: bulk verification, store codes, naming rules, location pages and governance.
excerpt: Managing many locations well is mostly a records problem: one source of truth, one owner per field, and a monthly check that catches drift before customers do.
imageAlt: Colorful push pins standing on a paper map in warm low sunlight
imageIdea: Real photo of push pins marking several places on a map, warm light, no brand names or logos.
author: The SocialDM Insights Team
bodyHtml:
To manage Google Business Profiles across many locations, keep every profile under one brand owned account, verify in bulk if you qualify, give each location a permanent store code, and keep names, categories, hours and location pages consistent from a single source of truth. Then write down who may change what, and check for drift every month.

Most multi location problems I see do not start as ranking problems. They start as records problems: a duplicate profile nobody remembers creating, a former manager who still owns a listing, hours that changed on the website but not on Google. This post covers the setup that prevents those, roughly in the order I would do it.

How does Google rank each location?

Google ranks each location on its own, using relevance, distance and prominence. A well known brand does not carry a thin profile in a given neighborhood, so every location has to be complete and accurate on its own terms.

Google's page on improving local ranking says businesses with complete and accurate information are more likely to show up in local results, that more reviews and positive ratings can help, and that there is no way to pay for a better local ranking. For a portfolio, that means the work multiplies by location count. The process matters more than any single tactic.

Can you verify many Google Business Profiles at once?

Yes, if you have 10 or more locations of the same business. Google offers bulk verification for chains through Business Profile Manager, and locations are not eligible to appear on Search or Maps until they are verified.

Google's bulk verification page notes that duplicate, suspended or disabled profiles do not count toward the 10 location minimum, so clean those up first. If you do not see a Verifications option, you may not have enough eligible profiles, and each location is verified individually. If your locations trade under different names, as many apartment communities do, confirm eligibility with Google before you plan a rollout around it.

What are store codes and why do they matter?

A store code is the unique ID you assign to each location so that Google, your spreadsheets and your internal systems all mean the same place. Pick a scheme once and never reuse or casually change a code.

Google's store code guidance says each location needs a unique code before you can import a bulk spreadsheet, that codes must be 64 characters or fewer, and that spreadsheet software can strip leading zeros, turning 0004 into 4. It also warns that changing a store code through a bulk upload on an existing location creates a duplicate, so edit codes in the profile's advanced settings instead. I prefer codes that match an ID your operations team already uses, such as a property or site number from accounting, so the same number appears in every report.

What should be the same at every location, and what should differ?

Naming format, category logic and brand facts should be the same everywhere. Address, phone, hours, photos, local attributes and the linked location page should be specific to each place.

Google's guidelines for representing your business say chain locations should use the same name within a country, that locations offering the same service should share a category, and that taglines and location details do not belong in the name. Locations that consistently use a different name on their signage and website can use that name, which is how most apartment communities work. Here is how I split the fields:

FieldSet centrallySet per location
Business nameNaming format, with no keywords or city addedLocation name if it is on signage and the website
CategoriesPrimary category by location typeSecondary categories that are true for that site
HoursHoliday hours calendarRegular and special hours
Website linkURL pattern and tracking parametersThe matching location page, not the home page
PhotosQuality and content rulesReal, current photos of that location
Store codeFormatThe code itself, which never changes

Does every location need its own page?

Yes. Each profile should link to a page about that location, and that page should say things no other page on your site says. A page that swaps a city name into a shared paragraph is not a location page.

Google's spam policies list pages targeted at specific regions or cities that funnel users to one page as an example of doorway abuse. A useful location page carries the address and hours that match the profile, directions and parking, what is offered at that site, who to contact there, and answers to the questions people ask about that place. We build these on a shared template so the structure is consistent, then fill in the local detail with someone who knows the location. The template is what makes scale possible. The local detail is what makes the page worth reading.

Who should own and edit the profiles?

The brand should own every profile through an organization controlled account, with location staff added as managers rather than owners. Write down who can change which fields and how changes are approved.

Google's page on owners and managers explains that a profile has one primary owner, that managers cannot add or remove users, and that new owners and managers wait 7 days before they can do some things, such as transferring primary ownership. The governance rules I would put in writing:

  • Ownership. Primary ownership sits with a brand account, never a personal email or a former vendor.
  • Field rights. Local teams can post updates, add photos and reply to reviews. Names, categories and website links change only through the central team.
  • Access reviews. Remove users when people leave, and review the full user list every quarter.
  • Change log. Record every central edit with a date, so you can tell your own changes from edits that came from somewhere else.
  • Escalation. Suspensions, duplicates and ownership disputes go to one named person.

How do you keep many locations accurate over time?

Run a monthly check that compares each profile against your source of truth and flags anything that drifted. Most errors come from changes nobody planned: an accepted outside edit, an hours change at one site, a new duplicate.

The check does not need to be elaborate. Export the profile data, compare it field by field to your master list, and review the differences before you push corrections. Then report by market, not just in total, because a portfolio average can hide one city where several locations have slipped. Our enterprise page describes how we run this across markets, and if AI answers are part of the question, our post on Google Business Profile and AI search covers how the two connect.

Questions we hear

How many locations do you need for Google Business Profile bulk verification?

Google offers bulk verification to businesses with 10 or more locations of the same business. Duplicate, suspended or disabled profiles do not count toward that minimum, so clean those up before you apply.

Can we change a location's store code?

Yes, in the profile's advanced settings. Do not change it through a bulk upload spreadsheet, because Google says that creates a duplicate location instead of updating the existing one.

Should we add the city to each location's business name?

No. Google's guidelines say location details and taglines do not belong in the business name. Put the city in the address and on the location page instead.

Should location managers own their Google Business Profiles?

Make them managers, not primary owners. Primary ownership should sit with a brand account so access survives staff and vendor changes.

How often should a multi location brand audit its profiles?

Monthly works for most portfolios, plus an extra check after any brand wide change such as new hours, a new category or a rebrand.
